heading: What each service language can use in the browser
body:
A service in Rust, Go, C#, F#, Kotlin, Java, Dart, Ruby or Swift runs in the page, but it does not call the browser itself. It reaches the browser only through Tachyon: the view reads its fields and calls its methods, events carry values in and out, and the storage annotations keep its data. Tachyon also gives every language a small set of browser APIs: `Clock`, `SecureRandom`, `Connectivity`, `PageVisibility`, `Preferences`, `Clipboard`, `Share`, `Notifications`, `Geolocation` and `WindowControls` (see the next sections and the feature "What a page may do to its window"). Other browser work, such as a request to the server, lives in a JavaScript or TypeScript service. That service publishes a typed event, and the service in the other language receives it with `OnEvent`.

The table shows what each language can use in the page. Tachyon's tests check every row.

| What | Rust | Go | C# | F# | Kotlin | Dart | Ruby | Swift | Java |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fields and methods for the view | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `publishEvent` and `OnEvent` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `Store` and caches | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `LocalState` and `SessionState` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `HTTPClient` sent by the browser | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No |
| `HTTPClient` sent by the Setup's HTTP adapter, with `Cached`, `ClearCache` and `UpdateCache` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No | Yes | Yes |
| `StreamRequest` and `SocketRequest` | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No | No |
| `Clock` and `SecureRandom` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `Connectivity`, `PageVisibility`, `Preferences` and their change events | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `Clipboard`, `Share`, `Notifications` and `Geolocation`, after a grant | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `WindowControls`, after a grant in `tac.application.window.controls` (a native window only; not in a service that the native app links in) | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| The current time from the language itself | No, use `Clock` | Yes | Yes | Yes, `System.DateTime.UtcNow` | Yes, `System.currentTimeMillis()` | Yes | Yes | No `Date` (no Foundation), use `Clock` | Yes, `System.currentTimeMillis()` |
| Random numbers from the language itself | No, use `SecureRandom` | Yes | Yes | Yes, `System.Random` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, `Int.random(in:)` | Yes, `java.util.Random` |
| Wait (sleep) | No | Yes, the page waits | Yes, the page waits | Yes, `Thread.Sleep` makes the page wait | Yes, `Thread.sleep` makes the page wait | Yes, in an `async` method | No | Yes, `Task.sleep` in an `async` method makes the page wait | No; only the wait of a `Retry` or a blocking `MaxAtOnce`, which makes the page wait |
| Console output | No | Yes | Yes | Yes, `printfn` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes, `print` | Yes, `System.out` |

Send requests from a JavaScript or TypeScript client. Its answers, and the messages of a stream or a socket, reach the other languages as typed events. In Rust, `std::time::SystemTime::now()` and `std::thread::sleep` stop the service with an error, and `println!` prints nothing. Use Tachyon's `Clock` and `SecureRandom` instead (see "Clock and secure random numbers"). Ruby refuses `sleep`, because a Ruby call must return before the page goes on.

Tachyon refuses code that calls the browser directly, and the build stops with `TY1317`: Go `syscall/js`; Dart `dart:js_interop`, `dart:js`, `dart:js_util`, `dart:html`, `package:web` and `package:js`; C# `System.Runtime.InteropServices.JavaScript`, `JSImport`, `JSExport` and `JSHost`; Rust `wasm_bindgen`, `web_sys`, `js_sys` and `wasm_import_module`; Kotlin `external`, `@JsFun`, `@JsExport`, `@JsModule`, `@JsName`, `js(…)`, `kotlinx.browser`, `org.w3c` and `kotlin.js`; Java `org.teavm`, `native` methods and TeaVM's `JS…` annotations such as `JSBody`, `JSObject` and `JSExport`; Ruby `TachyonWeb` and `JS`; and Swift `JavaScriptKit`, `JavaScriptEventLoop`, `JSObject`, `JSValue`, `JSClosure`, `JSPromise`, `@_extern` and `@_expose`. Such code breaks the test units of the language, and a native target has no browser. Tachyon's own code on the page is not checked.

In the example, `PlaceService` in JavaScript or TypeScript reads the browser and publishes a `PlaceFound` event. `MapService` receives the event with `OnEvent`, and the view shows its fields. Write `MapService` in any service language: the tabs show each one. The same pattern works for any browser API outside Tachyon's set.
